# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions month

## 1. Looking for "Competence Porn" movies where the characters are locked in

**Score:** 980
**Body:** I'm looking for movies where there's a group of people planning the HECK out of the problem they got themselves into, preferably hard science fiction but I'm open to other genres.

Something like:

* The Martian
* Project Hail Mary
* Interstellar ("It's impossible." "No, it's necessary.")
* All the planning scenes in Apollo 13, ESPECIALLY Apollo 13
* Tremors
* The 1st half of Oppenheimer

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Master and Commander. Boat competence. 
  - And ... Hunt for Red October. Submarine competence.
2. The Big Short
3. Sci fi, competence, but slightly different from your examples: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home

Edit: most of original and nineties Star Trek heavily feature the most competent characters in the galaxy solving seemingly impossible problems
4. Have you seen Contact and Contagion?  Not quite the same but still pretty smart. 
5. Sneakers
6. My Cousin Vinny 
  - Hell yeah. The scene when Marisa Tomei's character gets put on the stand is just so satisfying.
7. The Right Stuff
8. Would heist movies also scratch this itch? Like a little Ocean’s 11?

## 2. Wholesome movies like Project Hail Mary

**Score:** 804
**Body:** i suggested watching The Mist (2007) to my sweet boyfriend. He was so upset by the ending he very angrily left the room to splash his face with water and lay down while ranting how sick the writers must've been. he was a complete mess he just stared at the wall for a while. Meanwhile he loved project hail mary which i suggested a few weeks ago. is there another wholesome movie we can watch like project hail mary to kind of "wash" his anguish for The Mist away?

update: he was in a sour mood all day because of it and had been listening to the whinnie the pooh soundtrack. i really messed this poor guy up! 

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The Martian
  - The same author as Hail Mary
2. The secret life of walter mitty
  - Seconding this. Wonderful feel good flick with a killer soundtrack. 
3. Mrs. Harris goes to Paris. Surprisingly, everyone I have recommended this to, loves it- even my husband.  High dopamine, low stress.
4. Paddington 2
  - Also Paddington 1 is tremendously enjoyable 


5. * My Neighbor Totoro (animated fantasy-adventure)
* Amelie (romantic comedy)
* Good Will Hunting (drama)
* The Shawshank Redemption (drama)
* Rocky (drama)
* Muriel's Wedding (dramedy)
* Galaxy Quest (sci-fi comedy)
  - YESSSS GALAXY QUEST! I’m surprised I had to scroll this long to find it. What a gem.
6. Stardust

## 3. Movies that have no right being good?

**Score:** 563
**Body:** Hi! My friends and I have a weekly movie club and this week's theme is "somehow not terrible movies." We're trying to come up with 4-5 movies that sound like they would be god awful but are lowkey really good. I guess a semi-example is Warm Bodies?? like a zombie retelling of Romeo and Juliet should be terribleeee but it's actually pretty decent for a romcom. Our club is a bit more critically-acclaimed type movie focus though so maybe looking for something that is a step up from that? Essentially, we're looking for great movies with a terrible premise. Thanks!

1. Clue is based on a board game that you probably wouldn't watch somebody else playing, and incorporates a lot of the same game mechanics and details, but it's still super fun to watch. 
2. Lars and the Real Girl
3. Well known casts, but the concept sounds stupid:

Galaxy Quest

Down Periscope

Tremors
4. The Lego Movie
  - They made it *about* Lego. On a deep level.
5. Roadhouse. The original.
6. For this you want Swiss Army Man. A dude finds a corpse on the beach and rides him around like a jet ski powered by corpse farts.

And it’s so, so good.
  - They could do a Radcliffe double feature and also watch Guns Akimbo and a guy with guns bolted to his hands and forces to play in a game to the death. 
7. Safety Not Guaranteed 
8. Tucker and Dale vs Evil

## 4. Need a lesser known romcom for the girlfriend who has seen every movie I know of!

**Score:** 401
**Body:** OK, I like movies.  I by no means have seen them all and likely have seen less than most on this reddit.  But for the general population, I have a good knowledge and have seen many movies.

  
Well my girlfriend has me beat.  

  
So I said I would find us a good movie to watch, and as you my guess, she wants a romcom, and she has seen every movie I thought was good and recommended.

  
I told her I was coming to this board and was going to get a bunch of suggestions that would knock her socks off.  

  
A caveat to this is she does not want a foreign language film.  She wants it in english.  And also she doesn't want to go back before 1990 I would guess.

  
I will give you a list of her favorites but they are pretty standard.  I think everyone likes them.  

The Princess Bride.  Risky Business.  One fine day.  Pretty woman.  The proposal.  How to lose a guy in 10 days.

She doesn't like crude humor so she was not a fan of tropic thunder or  anchorman.

  
So please suggest a not widely known romcom that plays like a blockbuster.  Have at it and I anxiously await responses!

Added:  many are recommending about time.   She had seen it.   I started responding she has seen it but I am actually losing ground.   You guys are awesome.   The response has been simply amazing. 

She has seen most of the recommendations but some have stumped both of us and we are excited to watch. 

By the way,  she is fine with English films or aussie films. She just doesn't like to read subtitles. I will try to break her off that habit because there are some great foreign language films...

Additional:  well this response has blown me away.   We will sit down this weekend and we will have a look.   She had seen many of the recommendations and for most of the suggestions she said oh, that was really good. So you guys are recommending best movies!

If people want to find out how this little search turns out, how can I let you guys know?  Can I just add onto the body?  I'm not a reddit expert.   Some people post updates.   I could try to figure out how to do that. 

The response has been far over anything I thought would happen and I want to let you guys know what movie she hasn't seen!

More additional:  my goodness sometimes humanity surprises people.   As far as I am concerned this is the perfect example of when the internet works perfectly.   I was hoping to get a lead or 2 from the reddit crowd but you guys have come through in an amazing way.   I will say you guys have till Saturday to get your suggestions in. I am going to try to go through these suggestions with her over the weekend. This little thing about a guy who wanted to make his girl happy with some new romcoms had become my most viewed and most responded to post ever on reddit. Thank you all.   We will start to go through all the responses this weekend and i will post the winners.   This may be our own little romcom moment!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Stardust and if she’s ok with a pre 90s… Strictly Ballroom as a classic.
2. Blast from the Past (1999).
3. The American President 
  - Also Dave (1993)

Make it a double feature.
4. Palm Springs (2020)? I don’t think enough people saw this one and it’s fun.
5. The Big Sick
6. Fools rush in maybeeeeee?
7. Music and Lyrics 
8. The Truth About Cats and Dogs

Return to Me
9. Working Girl. A little old, but good. 

## 5. What is the ultimate "sit in silence and process it" movie you've ever watched?

**Score:** 381
**Body:** I’m chasing that rare cinematic feeling where a movie completely breaks your brain or leaves you shocked by the time the credits roll. The kind of film where the twist or the final scene is so huge, you need to sit in the dark for 10 minutes to recover.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. [The Zone of Interest (2023)](https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/the_zone_of_interest)
2. Gone baby gone. 

When I was 15, titanic affected me so badly emotionally that I spent the rest of my birthday silent and unable to interact with my friends haha. It was a mistake going to see that before having dinner out.

Not a movie but that tv series Behind Her Eyes. The plot twist of all plot twists EVER.
3. Requiem for a Dream easily tops that list for me
  - Was going to suggest this as well. A powerful movie that I never want to see again 🙂
4. Oldboy (2003) the twist left my jaw on the floor for the rest of the movie

Dear Zachary (2008) if documentaries count
  - Dear Zachary did not leave me in silence, it left me sobbing
    - I often recommend Dear Zachary with two bits of advice 1. don’t google it beforehand and 2. Watch it with someone because you will need to talk to someone afterwards. 
5. Seven, when it first came out. We were in a packed theater, and when the movie ended, no one moved or uttered a sound for quite a few seconds. 
6. Stalker or Solaris
7. come and see

## 3. Entire film studies could be done on Christopher Nolan’s interpretation of Agamemnon.

**Score:** 15850
**Body:** I feel like film classes could write whole essays on the way in which Christopher Nolan wrote and built up Agamemnon in his version of the Odyssey. The weight, the gravity of his being and his presence within Odysseus’s mind. Was he that big? Did he tower over others like the picture here? Or was this just how Odysseus had built him up in his mind?

He is the embodiment of politicians, particularly strongmen, since time immemorial. A facade of power and strength, cruel to those lesser than, only to be small and killed so easily bc he turned everyone against him.

Or is this monstrous figure in Odysseus’s mind the physical embodiment of his guilt? I must go to Troy because of Agamemnon, I’ve followed Agamemnon long enough, as excuses to lay his guilt on someone else?

Or was he truly this behemoth of a man? The king that held an army together on that beach for 10 years? Only to be humbled before Odysseus in death?

To me he’s the most fascinating character on the whole movie and he’s all three: the diminutive despot covering himself in the trappings of a god and pretending to be monstrous warrior, the specter who haunts Odysseus’s mind for embodying his shame over Troy, and the small man, who would do anything for power until all those who should cherish him learn to despise him.

Edit 1: as I think more on it: Agamemnon represented everything Odysseus was not and was afraid of becoming. He killed his child for wind, murdered by those he thought he loved. Yet in the end it was Odysseus who did the most monstrous thing of all. And Agamemnon standing at the gates right when they opened was the representation that he had become what he hated, and let the devils in both physically and mentally.

Edit 2: wow this post got bigger than I ever thought possible! A few other observations that others have pointed out that I agree with:

\- the golden spine hanging from his helmet, representative of how he himself did not have a spine. We never see him fight. His own brother lives in the shit and squalor of the Trojan horse while he never draws a sword.

\-people have complained about his voice, but that was the point, to show how small, insignificant, and equal to all he was in death. Sacrificed his child, led an army of 1,000 ships for 10 years for what? To be equal in death as the lowly farmers son, drinking with his hand from a small pool atop an overturned shield.

\-his armor is ridiculous and too large and out of place. That was intentional. Again, are we seeing what he actually was? Or how Odysseus remembered him to be? The Odyssey itself was an oral story for centuries before it was written down and Nolan chose to show the entire story in someone telling another a story. Perhaps we never see his face bc of Odysseus’s shame at what he’d done, a man who loved his family, breaking Zeus’s law to such an extent that he ends the Bronze Age. Perhaps he was afraid he would see his own face if he removed the helmet in his memory.

Edit 3: this is crazy! I’ve never had any post get big! I’m just a nobody, so to be able to share my interpretation and have so many others share there’s is awesome! 

What do others think?

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. ![gif](giphy|sDOhzJBsFvjMY)
  - https://i.redd.it/3vxernsiwieh1.gif

  - Scrolled down for this. God bless you

We really only ever see Agamemnon in Odysseus's memories, mostly shared with Calypso, where we see all the over the top fantastical elements, which can be interpreted as representations of his trauma. I think it's perfectly reasonable to argue we're seeing Agamemnon as he remembers him within that trauma, not as an accurate representation.
3. I’ve seen some people complain about his voice, or the fact that it’s Benny Safdie. That, to me, is the whole idea. He’s treated as this god, when really he is just a man under his armor. The armor makes him what he is. 

That’s why I loved the scene when he speaks to Odysseus in the underground; it’s not this deep growling voice; it’s normal, it’s human. 

Lastly, they never show his face when he is killed, just a quick side profile and his hair. The movie even helps build on the illusion. 
  - I also noticed we never see Agamemnon actually fight, or even unsheathe his sword.  He’s standing RIGHT in front of the gates of Troy when they open (menacingly), and he starts striding right in, and he stays right on the forefront of the fight the entire time, but he operates solely via his men who rush all around him.  We’re not given the distinct impression that he’s weak, or afraid, or anything like that, but we’re left with a lot to ponder about Agamemnon and Odysseus’s view of him.
    - Totally this! 

When you first see him, it's at the end of taking down Troy and they're all ready to go home, and everyone looks like they've been through hell. 

Agamemnon's armor is pristine. 

At the end when we finally see all the destruction, there's a quick shot of him walking around with a body guard on either side. 

Even in Hades, he barely dips his fingers in the blood. Like he doesn't want to get his hands dirty.


Really, the only different between him and Robert Pattinson's character screaming at everyone else to fight for his own ambitions is presentation. 
      - And he fucking floats in Hades, like he's not picking up his feet and moving.

## 4. The Odyssey (2026) Review - IMAX is Officially a Trojan Horse

**Score:** 13993
**Body:** I went into this film with no pre-formed opinion. I didn't want to jump on the hate bandwagon before seeing it. Nolan has never made a truly bad movie ever. I've been entertained by almost everything he's made. So I went in open-minded.

Let me get the controversial stuff out of the way. The casting, modern English, modern accents, and historical inaccuracies didn't take me out of it one bit. I was completely fine with all of that.

My problem with this movie is it simply didn't have that "wow" factor.

Dinosaurs hit the big screen in 1993. There was nothing mind blowing about the cyclops or giants.

*Game of Thrones* and *House of the Dragon* offer more immersive and visually breathtaking visuals from the fantasy genre. *The Northman* had a far superior siege sequence than the siege of Troy, not to mention photography. On that note...

I was completely unimpressed by the photography. Worst of Nolan’s career. What’s the point of shooting large format if all you’re gonna do is shoot tight, shallow, crammed, darkly lit, claustrophobic, shoulder-mount camera shake shots?

The score was forgettable. So were the set pieces generally. And my god, the sound effects were bad. Every time I heard a sword stabbing or slitting someone, it just took me out. Pretty sure they just pulled sound effects from movies 20 years old. For a $250m movie, record some fresh fucking sound effects.

John Leguizamo and Samantha Morton gave the best performances in the movie.

There were some sequences I found quite engaging. I don't want to spoil it, but my favorite scene was mainly anchored by Elliot Page and had a truly absorbing atmosphere and tone to it.

The best element of the movie was the relationship between Damon and Himesh Patel. That should have been the primary focus of the story in my opinion.

I’m drawing a line in the sand right now. I have little further interest in movies shot in IMAX. I like large format, but I want a wide screen image. Would rather more movies just get shot in Alexa LF. I don't particularly love this movie, but *Roma* is a better example of what large format photography should look like.

You can’t have agile, high energy action sequences on IMAX like *Die Hard 3* \- taxi raging through Central Park. Everything has to be really stiff. If you give audiences *The Odyssey's* ocean sequences and have them watch back to back with *Master and Commander's* ocean sequences, I’d love to know what they think is more visually immersive and gripping. I'm willing to bet it's the latter.

**3/5.**

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm month

## 1. The Obsession discourse and how people will prioritize moral superiority over critical understanding.

**Score:** 1665
**Body:** A very large amount of the Obsession discourse revolves around the character of Bear and how, despite being the protagonist, he is clearly the most evil character in the story. Any half intelligent person who watched Obsession can agree that Bear does some pretty terrible things, and is overall a pathetic, bad person, but at the same time, the film portrays him with a level of complexity that a lot of people like to ignore. Bear does not start out as a clearly bad person. His first few nights with possessed Nikki, he is as respectful as he possibly could be in that situation and is clearly very uncomfortable. Only as the movie progresses do we see his true colors and that his morals very easily go away in favor of his lust and need for validation.   
But a lot of the discussion of Obsession has stopped treating Bear like a somewhat complex character and instead has become a contest on how much you can condemn Bear. Bear isn’t treated like the somewhat complex character je is, and is instead treated like an irredeemable monster. If you show any sympathy to this character, people will hound you for defending a rapist. Bear is meant to be sympathized with. The point of the film is that we all have a bit of Bear in us. Bear isn’t a scary, terrible villain, he’s your friend, your relative, even potentially you. The scariest part of Bear is that he’s kind of relatable at times. But because saying you relate to Bear makes you look bad, people try to do the opposite and when discussing Obsession, make sure to dwell on how terrible Bear is as if to say “I could never be like him, he’s so evil, I could never be evil I’m just a normal guy.”

I think something comparable is the discourse of The Zone of Interest. A good amount of people criticized this movie for humanizing Nazis but the whole point of that movie was that nazis are human and that, in the right circumstances we could all potentially be nazis. Nazis weren’t monsters, they were people. Bear is Obsessions Nazis. He is meant to show us that anybody could do terrible things, but instead of looking inward, people look for a moral high ground and refuse to identify with Bear.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. >But because saying you relate to Bear makes you look bad, people try to do the opposite and when discussing Obsession, make sure to dwell on how terrible Bear is as if to say “I could never be like him, he’s so evil, I could never be evil I’m just a normal guy.”

I can picture Slavoj Zizek (watch *Perverts Guide to Cinema* if you haven't) saying something along the lines of "people think the horror is freaky Nikki's violent and extreme obsession. But the real horror is in knowing you could be Bear." As you mention, that idea is scary enough that many viewers choose to outright deny the possibility.
  - I can hear it in his voice
    - >I can hear it in his voice

Sniffs.
2. I take it as Bear is just a symbol of mankind. Humanity is willing to turn a blind eye for convenience at every meaningful turn in both our history, and present. I didn't take him as a cartoonish like character. I found him extremely relatable, and obviously detestable at the same time. 
3. Anyone criticizing Zone of Interest for humanizing nazis is an idiot and should be ignored.  The whole point is to emphasize the banality of evil - that nazis were just people who did their laundry, had lovers quarrels, and bickered over what was for dinner.  That is the entire fucking point.  To show that they weren't boogeymen and that if you go through your life only afraid of boogeymen, you may find yourself in a world with gas chambers.
  - Plus in like the opening scene they’re basically looting the belongings of dead Jews and the wife is shown to be cruel to the servants. The film didn’t try to make the Nazis particularly likable or even relatable, just showed them living their day to day.
4. One thing I've found interesting is how quickly people will dismiss the actual movie to come up with wild theories that are easily proven false by paying attention to the movie. I don't think this is unique to Obsession, just more prevalent due to its success.   
For example, Bear did not murder his cat to get sympathy from Nikki. Everything in the movie points to it being an accident due to his negligence (and tbh, if you've ever had a cat you know you can't even get them to eat the pills your vet told you to give them, so it's frankly, a bad scene). In the subsequent scene, he tells Nikki he doesn't want to go out but doesn't even mention the cat. He only goes out because she pushes him to. If he'd killed his cat to get her attention, wouldn't he have called her? Or told her immediately? Like, wheeeeere are you people getting this?  
I also think he made the wish never believing it would or could come true, agree about the respectful behavior in his home the first night, and also think he dismissed her behavior initially because she told him she was being weird because she drank and took drugs, which is more believable than a weird wish stick from the witchy shop worked.   
Bear becomes the villain when presented with an opportunity to sleep with her fully knowing it isn't her. He's awful, but he's garden-variety awful, not some supervillain who orchestrated his cat's murder and stole her crystal necklace to make her susceptible to magic.   
It's certainly been interesting to see such widespread discourse and how differently some people interpret things, I'll give it all that. 
  - Also Nikki only finds out about his Cat through Sarah 
5. At this point there are more posts about the discourse around this movie than there are posts actually discussing the movie. 

I really can't say I understand the growing trend here of these "response" posts, where the people you're responding to won't necessarily even see this post. So people who don't necessarily hold the opinions you're pushing back on are left to respond instead. And then perhaps in a few days someone will read this post and create their own post responding to it, which you will not see, and the chain will continue, an endless loop of responses where nobody is actually talking to each other.
6. Sure, I think part of what makes Bear an interesting character is how people can identify elements of his shittiness within themselves. But also, yeah, if you say "I really identify with this Bear guy" in public, people are gonna look at you weird, the way they would if (to use your own analogy) you had said "I really identified with those people in The Zone of Interest." 

But I also have to object to your read of Bear. To say he's "as respectful as possible" to Nikki while she's possessed is... not accurate imo. At minimum, she seems to be having a mental health crisis of some kind, and he overlooks that to sleep with her immediately.

You say he's not scary, he's your friend or relative. I think the reason the movie has struck such a chord is that he is realistically identifiable as _both_ scary _and_ your friend, relative, etc. It is a scary and threatening concept to a lot of women that their so-called male friends might willfully deprive them of their autonomy and identify for their own gratification, and I don't know how you'd convince someone who finds the movie scary for that reason would view Bear some redeemable guy. He doesn't lose his morals, he just didn't have them, and even as the situation deteriorates in the movie, he doesn't try to actually set things right until all other selfish options have been exhausted.

## 2. Another Odyssey take: modern morality is boring

**Score:** 1325
**Body:** The film is undoubtedly impressive and accomplished in its construction, inspiring awe more in the way of a great feat of architecture than in the way of great drama. Not unlike the Trojan horse, but with rather less substance contained within its sleek, polished hull.

I have a lot of issues with this movie, and I’ll get to those, but what keeps the movie from being a failure, in my view, is the production. The world is beautifully realized. Whatever my wishes for a historically accurate Bronze Age recreation, once the movie started, I was never taken out of it. Even Agamemnon’s 3D-printed looking-ass helmet worked for me. And the fantastical elements are incredibly well-imagined. The cyclops, Circe’s magic, the trip to Hades, the sirens—all of it looked really fucking cool. On top of all that is the score and sound design, powerfully atmospheric, more sombre than epic. 

Specifically in terms of production—that is, recreating a semi-historical/semi-mythological setting with this level of imagination and detail—the comparison I found myself making was to Robert Eggers’ *The Northman*. But that is also where my main issue with Nolan’s *Odyssey* begins. What I admire so much about *The Northman*, beyond its world-building, is its commitment to preserving the morality of its setting. That is, when Alexander Skarsgård chooses vengeance and a warrior’s death over his family, he is not penalized for it by the narrative; any viking man worth his beard would have made the same choice, and thus he is brought to eternal glory in Valhalla. 

*The Odyssey*, by contrast, persistently imposes utterly modern ethical concerns on its source material. The original Odysseus is not a hero because he is virtuous, but because he’s a genius badass—he fights dirty and cheats (in both senses of the word), and we still root for him because he’s a fun hang. We are impressed when he devises the plan to escape the Cyclops, and can’t help but laugh as he arrogantly turns back to declare his true name, so that the conquered beast may know its conqueror. Nolan’s Odysseus is morally unimpeachable, but seldom impressive or entertaining. The reason for this seems to be Nolan’s concern with preserving audience investment in his character, but ends up having the opposite effect. Nearly every other character is more interesting, which is a problem when the character’s name is the name of the movie. Robert Pattinson’s Antinous in particular—at once the most despicable and the most captivating.

I am reminded of an interview with Martin Scorsese following the release of *The Wolf of Wall Street*. Scorsese laughed off critics who felt the film lacked a moral center, asking in response: “Do you really need me to tell you that that stuff is wrong?” In the film, we’re not rooting for Jordan Belfort because he is a hero, but because, again, he’s a fun hang. Unlike Scorsese, Nolan doesn’t seem to trust that audiences will accept the source material’s ambiguity. Nor does he seem to think us capable, unless he spells it out for us, of understanding that war is, in fact, bad. This Odysseus simply won’t shut up about how sorry he is about the sack of Troy. Like Oppenheimer in *Oppenheimer*, he’s a war-time genius who apparently did not realize what the consequences of his invention might be before it was too late. My eyeballs did a full backwards 360 when Odysseus, reflecting on how the war accelerated the decline of the Mycenaeans, says something to the effect of, “We were the sea people all along,” a line seemingly sprung from the same writing workshop as Guillermo del Toro’s *Frankenstein*, see: “No, Victor, YOU are the monster.” 

To this end, virtually every single female character in the story is turned into a victim of endless patriarchal cruelty. Helen and Clytemnestra are both violently punished for their acts of rebellion against their husbands. Circe seems to suffer under the trauma of some unspecified violence done to her in the past. Athena is turned from the poem’s steely-eyed spiritual guide into a meek symbol for the cost of men’s violence, the embodiment of wisdom literally and metaphorically beheaded during the sack of Troy. It is certainly an interesting choice by Nolan to have this goddess, perhaps the most powerful presence in the poem, forced to her knees by two men… The only exception is Calypso, but only because she isn’t really a character at all. The cumulative effect is a story in which women exist to illustrate male violence, rather than as individuals in their own right.

Anne Hathaway’s Penelope has moments that gesture toward greater depth, but they are few and far between, and never amount to much of anything. Her character, along with Hathaway’s performance, is at their best when communicating the frustration of being a woman in a world where what ought to be rightfully yours is denied you, in favor of less competent men. She seems more tempted by the wiles of Antinous, the head-suitor, than Odysseus by any of the women he encounters, and at one point I was wondering if she really wanted him to come home at all. But all that goes out the window once he does arrive on the scene, and the movie acts as though she has been the unambiguously dutiful wife of Homer’s text all along.

Nolan’s *Odyssey* is ultimately a profoundly Anglo-American take on this story, in which the violence wrought by great powers upon the rest of the world is seen through the eyes of someone who represents those same powers, redeemed only because he feels bad about it. It’s Oliver Stone’s *Platoon* all over again, a film in which the greater tragedy of the Vietnam War is not the fate of the Vietnamese, but that of the poor Americans who realized it was bad to murder and rape, and only after they were through with it. 

Still, none of this is enough to make *The Odyssey* a bad film. Nolan remains too accomplished a filmmaker for that. The craft on display—the production design, the creature work, Ludwig Göransson’s mournful score, the sheer confidence with which this world is realized—is often breathtaking. My frustration is that a film of such extraordinary imagination in its visuals proves so unimaginative in its ideas. It recreates Homer’s world with remarkable conviction, only to flatten its moral and psychological strangeness into something far more familiar.

5. The main question surrounding Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey is not whether the film accurately represents the morality of the Bronze Age. It is also not simply a question of whether Nolan has turned Odysseus into a hero who feels too modern. The more important question is what Nolan is trying to preserve from Homer. This is the point where the difference between your criticism of the film and its actual artistic intention becomes clear in my opinion.

Many critics like yours understand Odysseus primarily as an antihero. He is not a figure who gains admiration through moral purity. He succeeds because of his intelligence, his ability to deceive, and his willingness to take risks. He tricks his enemies, manipulates situations, and survives through his ability to think beyond those around him. These qualities are what make him fascinating. The Odysseus of the epic is not a modern hero who is admired because he is a good person. He is admired because he is extraordinary.

This interpretation is valid, but it only describes one aspect of the character. The Odyssey is not one of the most important works in literary history because it tells the story of an exceptionally clever adventurer. Its importance comes from the larger question it explores: what does human greatness actually mean and what dangers exist within it?  
Odysseus is a man who can overcome almost any situation through his intelligence. At the same time, his abilities repeatedly bring him into conflict with his own arrogance. The same quality that allows him to succeed also creates many of his problems. His greatest strength is connected to his greatest weakness.

This is the foundation of Nolan’s approach. His interest is not only whether Odysseus remains an engaging character. He is interested in what a hero represents when the consequences of his actions are taken seriously. The criticism that Nolan places a modern morality onto Homer therefore misunderstands the film. He does not simply replace an ancient worldview with a modern one. Instead, he focuses on a conflict that already exists within Homer’s epic: the tension between glory and guilt, victory and destruction, civilization and barbarism.  
This becomes especially visible in the structure of the film. A common criticism is that Nolan has transformed the Odyssey into a modern and morally instructive hero’s journey. His approach is actually much closer to Homer’s own narrative method. The Odyssey is not a classical hero’s journey in the modern Hollywood sense. It does not follow a simple line in which a hero leaves home, faces challenges, changes, and finally achieves victory. Homer tells the story through episodes, memories, and interruptions. The narrative constantly shifts. The past enters the present and individual stories appear within the larger story.

The literary scholar Erich Auerbach described this quality of Homer’s writing as the complete presence of the world being portrayed. Homer does not force every scene toward one final climax. Each moment receives its own space and each encounter has its own meaning. Nolan uses a similar structure. The episodes of the journey are not only obstacles that stand between Odysseus and his return home. They become separate experiences that examine different aspects of human existence.  
Through this approach, the film challenges the traditional Hollywood idea of heroism. Nolan is not mainly telling the story of a man who becomes greater because of his struggles. He is telling the story of a man whose greatness becomes increasingly difficult to defend.

This can also be seen in the way Nolan presents the famous mythological scenes. In the case of Circe, there would have been an easy solution. The transformation of the men into pigs could have been shown through modern digital effects. Instead, Nolan chooses a physical and almost ancient form of filmmaking. The transformation happens through touch, movement, and editing. The audience does not simply observe an effect. They experience the process of transformation itself. The scene suggests that cinema is not defined by perfectly reproducing reality, but by shaping the way the viewer perceives reality.

The same idea appears in the encounter with the Sirens. Nolan avoids the obvious choice of presenting their song as a spectacular visual and sensory experience. Instead, he removes that experience from the audience. The sound is reduced and perception becomes limited. The viewer is placed in a position similar to Odysseus. They know that something attractive and dangerous exists, but they cannot fully experience it.  
This decision connects to the famous interpretation of the Siren episode by Horkheimer and Adorno, who understood it as an early representation of a central problem of modern society. Odysseus wants to experience the power of the Sirens, but he can only do so by having himself tied to the mast. His workers continue rowing because they cannot hear the song. The ruler is allowed to experience temptation, but only under the condition that he loses the ability to act. The scene already contains a contradiction that defines the modern world. Humanity seeks freedom while also creating systems to control everything that could make that freedom dangerous.  
Nolan transforms this idea into a reflection on cinema itself. The viewer is also limited. They can see the images, but they cannot enter them. They can witness overwhelming experiences, but they cannot directly participate in them. The film is therefore not only about Odysseus. It is also about the relationship between people and images, desire, and control.  
From this perspective, the political dimension of the film becomes clearer. Nolan is not simply presenting the basic message that war is wrong. Such an interpretation would be too simple. The deeper question is what happens when a civilization no longer recognizes its own violence as violence.

The central realization of the film is that the barbarians may not be outsiders. They may be ourselves. Odysseus is not only the hero who fights against a dangerous world. He is also the representative of a civilization that becomes destructive in the name of order and superiority.  
This is where the connection to Oppenheimer becomes visible. Both films focus on exceptional individuals whose abilities allow them to create something that changes history. At the same time, both characters must discover that greatness does not automatically create moral justification. Oppenheimer splits the atom and transforms the world. Odysseus destroys Troy and becomes a hero. Yet both figures must confront the fact that their greatest achievements contain a destructive element.  
Nolan’s earlier films explore similar questions. In the Batman trilogy, the Joker and Bane represent figures who reject all forms of order and place themselves above every law. In Odyssey, Antinous serves a comparable role. He is not simply a villain. He represents a form of power that accepts no higher authority. Nolan contrasts this with the idea of Zeus’ law. This law does not only represent divine power. It represents the principle that even the most powerful individuals must remain subject to rules.  
This is the political ambiguity at the center of the film. Nolan is not arguing against every form of order. He believes in institutions, law, and social structures (he is old conservative liberal after all… poor dude). At the same time, he shows how dangerous it becomes when those responsible for protecting an order place themselves outside of it.

This is why Odysseus does not become a traditional triumphant hero at the end of the story. His return home is not presented as a simple victory. He returns as a man who has to recognize that his glory was achieved at a cost. The tragedy is not that he eventually discovers that war is destructive. The tragedy is that he realizes his own greatness was connected to the destruction he caused.

From this perspective, Nolan’s Odyssey is not a simplification of Homer through modern moral ideas. It is a specific interpretation of the epic. It does not only ask why people admire extraordinary individuals. It also asks why people are so willing to follow them.

The film is less interested in the hero as a figure who achieves victory. Its focus lies on the moment when the hero has to understand what that victory actually represents

2. Moments of criticism like this have always been my favorite. I double-majored in English Lit and Film Production in college, and conversations about adaptations put my literary sensibilities at odds with my admiration of film as a practical craft.  Do you judge a film adaptation by its ability to bring something insightful about the original text to screen in a way at least somewhat loyal to the original? Or do you judge it as a film on its own merits and disregard anything that came before it?

Hitchcock famously said he never adapted classic novels because of the screentime it takes to do them well, and instead went for more plot-driven pulp fare as his source material. "What I do is to read a story only once, and if I like the basic idea, I just forget all about the book and start to create cinema." I think of this quote every time I watch another adaptation of The Odyssey, *O Brother Where Art Thou*, which I think uses this approach to perfection to shirk the responsibility of adapting one of the most studied pieces of literature with any sort of fidelity.

The tension we see in Wilson's review (which I don't think is "scathing" so much as slightly disappointed) seems to come from the fact that Nolan chose a murky in-between. His adaptation is neither a 20-hour diligent adaptation of the original epic, nor is it a Hitchcockian imaginative leap that ignores all but the bones of the original. Instead, he lets himself do both and neither. There are moments like the line of axes and the stringing of Odysseus's bow that felt like the page sprung to life and moments where he anachronistically borrows from much later texts like when Menelaus quotes a line written two millenia later by saying "the face that launched a thousand ships." Then there are moments where he takes wild departures from the original, such as showing a disfigured Helen, because it's a cinematically visual way to show the decades-long journey she's been on in only a few seconds.

  
I understand and agree with almost all of Emily Wilson's criticisms. I largely find Nolan films to be overrated and went into this expecting to roll my eyes. And yet, I absolutely loved the film.

Nolan is letting go of all those almost Brechtian tendencies he has for emotionally distancing the viewer from the character, and letting his work be clumsy and emotionally vulnerable in a way that elevates it above many of his previous films.

Penetration with sharp objects itself should be PG-13. To get an R, consider if the aftermath of the wound is shown, if there’s visible blood during penetration and the amount, if it’s a close-up shot vs. wide shot, and how much time spent on the shot. 



If the same battle used Star Wars lightsabers and blaster rifles instead of metal arrows, it’s PG-13. But because of the technicality that arrows exist and they’re sharp, an orange considered. The weapon choice is an absolutely an insane determinate.

All visible evidence point to the sign that Nolan was at least trying to make a PG-13 film when filming this, by how many times the film actually held back by NOT showing you the thing, but at the end of the day, said “Screw it, I’m a brand” rather than shave 20 seconds off the movie for resubmission. 



It’s frankly pathetic that this an R. The MPAA should be the most lenient with content in film as compared to Northern European countries, but instead the American system is closer to Sharia Law. 



The content shown here is what I’d expect and desire from a dark PG-13 comic book film. This is a family friendly movie; it’s on the very dark side of a family friendly movie, but it’s a family friendly movie a family of two parents and two tweens can enjoy. If this gets the same rating as Last House on the Left, America has a serious rating problem. America needs to desensitises itself to what it considers mature content.
